newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels practice with captured tanks.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels practice with captured tanks.

text.p: Albanian rebels, in arms against President Sali Berisha, practised manoeuvres in at least a dozen tanks at a captured army base in this southern village on Saturday.
Former base commander Major Ilir Kermezi and scores of his soldiers switched sides to join the rebels after anti-government riots swept this region near the Greek border last weekend.
A Reuters correspondent saw at least 12 old Chinese-built tanks manoeuvring around the Bajkaji base. Kermezi said 25 tanks at the base were in working condition.
He showed off hundreds of shells for tank cannons during a tour of the base 20 km (12 miles) into the hills above the rebel-held port of Sarande.
He also displayed thousands of rounds of smaller calibre ammunition for assault rifles, anti-aircraft guns and rocket launchers. Dozens of barrels of petrol were at a base depot for the tanks.

"We tell Berisha to come down and seize southern Albania if he dares but he won't find a single soldier in the south who supports him," said Sopot Devvish, a former army lieutenant at the base who has joined the rebel cause.
Villages in the rugged hills around Bajkaji were supplying food to the base for the ex-soldiers. Rebels have set up camps in the hills and thrown up dozens of roadblocks in the region.
Southern Albania has been swept by anti-government protests and riots since January when popular, but fraudulent, savings schemes collapsed, wiping out the savings of many families.
Anger has focused on Berisha for allowing the unregulated "pyramid" schemes to flourish and for failing to warn investors of their dangers.
"We want our money back. We worked like dogs in Greece. I had three million drachmas ($12,500) in the pyramids," said Sopot. "We will take anybody but Berisha."
The self-styled rebels, whose main demands are that they get their money back and that Berisha quit, have control of most of the country from the coastal port of Vlore to the Greek border.

Gjirokaster, a barracks town about 30 km (20 miles) from the border, is the main government stronghold in the area. Some tanks venture out from Gjirokaster to take up positions on the roads but soldiers let cars pass freely.

Berisha has given the rebels until Sunday to surrender their weapons in return for an amnesty but there has been no sign of compliance. All efforts are focused on preparing defences for a showdown with the army.
In Sarande, rebel gunmen fired shots in the air on Saturday to drive off a crowd trying to board the lone ferry operating to this embattled southern Albanian port.
Several hundred people swarmed around the "Kaliopi" when it arrived with supplies from the nearby Greek island of Corfu. The ferry can carry about 100 people.
The rebels fired warning shots to drive the crowd back so supplies could be unloaded and three people wounded in a gunfight with suspected secret police on Friday evacuated.
Three rebels were wounded, two seriously, when a car ran their checkpoint in Xare, just inside the Greek border south of Sarande.
The rebels said three men in the car were scouting the area for a possible move by the army to regain control of Sarande and other towns.

Rebels seized Sarande, Delvine, Tepelene and other towns and villages in anti-government rioting last week. They seized large stocks of weapons from state arsenals, including artillery and tanks, and joined the revolt which began in the port of Vlore.

Rebels in Tepelene have set up headquarters in the town hall to co-ordinate efforts to resist government troops. The army has vanished since a fight with rebels near Delvine, east of Sarande, on Wednesday.
Weapons in Tepelene as well as other towns were being taken away from children.

Outside the home of a teenager who was shot dead in Tepelene -- either by accident or in an exchange of fire at a roadblock -- two Kalashnikov rifles were tied together, a message from his family to Berisha that the boy's death would be avenged.
